An irrational xxx is a Liouville number if for every m≥1m \ge 1m≥1 there are infinitely many integer pairs (p,q)(p, q)(p,q) with q≥2q \ge 2q≥2 satisfying ∣x−p/q∣<1/qm|x - p/q| < 1/q^m∣x−p/q∣<1/qm. For k≥1k \ge 1k≥1 put Uk=⋃q≥2⋃p∈Z(p/q−1/qk, p/q+1/qk)U_k = \bigcup_{q \ge 2}\bigcup_{p \in \mathbb{Z}} (p/q - 1/q^k,\ p/q + 1/q^k)Uk​=⋃q≥2​⋃p∈Z​(p/q−1/qk, p/q+1/qk).

(a) Show each UkU_kUk​ is a dense open set in R\mathbb{R}R. (b) Show G=⋂k≥1Uk∩⋂j≥1(R∖{rj})G = \bigcap_{k \ge 1} U_k \cap \bigcap_{j \ge 1} (\mathbb{R} \setminus \{r_j\})G=⋂k≥1​Uk​∩⋂j≥1​(R∖{rj​}), where {rj}\{r_j\}{rj​} enumerates the rationals, is a GδG_\deltaGδ​ set all of whose elements are Liouville numbers. (c) Use the Baire category theorem to conclude the Liouville numbers are dense in R\mathbb{R}R and uncountable.

Uk=⋃q≥2⋃p∈Z(pq−1qk, pq+1qk)U_k = \bigcup_{q \ge 2}\bigcup_{p \in \mathbb{Z}} \left(\frac{p}{q} - \frac{1}{q^k},\ \frac{p}{q} + \frac{1}{q^k}\right)Uk​=q≥2⋃​p∈Z⋃​(qp​−qk1​, qp​+qk1​)
G=⋂k≥1Uk ∩ ⋂j≥1(R∖{rj})G = \bigcap_{k \ge 1} U_k \ \cap\ \bigcap_{j \ge 1} (\mathbb{R} \setminus \{r_j\})G=k≥1⋂​Uk​ ∩ j≥1⋂​(R∖{rj​})
  • Baire Category Theorem
Show solution

  1. (a) Each UkU_kUk​ is a union of open intervals, hence open. Every rational p/qp/qp/q lies in the interval centered at itself, so Q⊂Uk\mathbb{Q} \subset U_kQ⊂Uk​; since Q\mathbb{Q}Q is dense, each UkU_kUk​ is dense.

  2. (b) GGG is a countable intersection of open sets, hence GδG_\deltaGδ​ (each R∖{rj}\mathbb{R} \setminus \{r_j\}R∖{rj​} is open too). Let x∈Gx \in Gx∈G. Then xxx is irrational, and for each kkk there is a pair (pk,qk)(p_k, q_k)(pk​,qk​) with ∣x−pk/qk∣<1/qkk|x - p_k/q_k| < 1/q_k^k∣x−pk​/qk​∣<1/qkk​.

    If only finitely many distinct pairs occurred, some pair (p,q)(p, q)(p,q) would repeat for infinitely many kkk, forcing ∣x−p/q∣=0|x - p/q| = 0∣x−p/q∣=0, i.e. x=p/qx = p/qx=p/q, contradicting irrationality. So infinitely many distinct pairs occur. For fixed mmm, the pairs with k≥mk \ge mk≥m satisfy ∣x−pk/qk∣<1/qkk≤1/qkm|x - p_k/q_k| < 1/q_k^k \le 1/q_k^m∣x−pk​/qk​∣<1/qkk​≤1/qkm​, so xxx meets the definition of a Liouville number.

  3. (c) GGG is a countable intersection of dense open sets, so by the Baire category theorem it is dense in R\mathbb{R}R; hence so are the Liouville numbers. Moreover GGG is uncountable: if G={xn}G = \{x_n\}G={xn​} were countable, then G∩⋂n(R∖{xn})=∅G \cap \bigcap_n (\mathbb{R} \setminus \{x_n\}) = \varnothingG∩⋂n​(R∖{xn​})=∅ would be a countable intersection of dense open sets, hence dense by Baire — a contradiction.

With x=∑2an3−nx = \sum 2a_n 3^{-n}x=∑2an​3−n and y=∑2bn3−ny = \sum 2b_n 3^{-n}y=∑2bn​3−n, we have x,y∈Cx, y \in Cx,y∈C and

    x+y=∑n=1∞2(an+bn)3n=2∑n=1∞en3n=s.x + y = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{2(a_n + b_n)}{3^n} = 2\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{e_n}{3^n} = s.x+y=n=1∑∞​3n2(an​+bn​)​=2n=1∑∞​3nen​​=s.

  3. Hence s∈C+Cs \in C + Cs∈C+C. Since sss was arbitrary, [0,2]⊂C+C[0, 2] \subset C + C[0,2]⊂C+C, and the two inclusions give C+C=[0,2]C + C = [0, 2]C+C=[0,2].
